Long week, and I want to get it all down before I forget what actually happened versus what I think happened.

Monday started badly. I planned three hours for the CS4680 homework and told myself I'd be done by dinner. I sat down at two, opened the assignment, and then spent almost forty minutes "setting up," which really meant reorganizing my notes folder, renaming files, and reading the rubric twice without writing anything. When I finally started, the first part went fast. The prompt patterns section was easy because we covered persona and few-shot in lecture and I had examples ready. The code part was where everything slowed down. I kept running into a JSON parsing error that turned out to be the model wrapping its answer in code fences. I lost a full hour to that, and when I fixed it I felt stupid for not checking the raw output first. Lesson: print the raw response before assuming my parser is wrong.

Tuesday I had a shift at work from four to nine, and I didn't plan for how tired I'd be afterward. I had "read chapter five" on my list for after the shift, and of course it didn't happen. I sat on my bed with the book open for twenty minutes and absorbed nothing. I should stop scheduling reading after work. Reading needs the most attention of anything I do, and I keep putting it in the slot where I have the least.

Wednesday was the best day. I went to the library at nine in the morning, put my phone in my bag on silent, and did two focused blocks before lunch. The difference was huge. In the first block I finished the calculus problems I'd been avoiding, and in the second I outlined the English essay. I think the library works because there's nothing else to do there. At home there's always something, like laundry or my roommate or the fridge. I want to make Wednesday mornings a fixed thing, maybe even add Saturday mornings.

Thursday I had the physics lab report. I estimated ninety minutes because I thought the writing would be quick, but the data analysis took longer than the entire writing section. We had to fit a curve to our pendulum measurements and explain why the fit was off at large angles. I didn't understand the small-angle approximation well enough to explain it, so I had to go back to the textbook and then to a video. By the time I understood it, I'd been at it for two hours and hadn't written a word of the discussion. I finished at eleven at night. The report is fine, I think, but I was rushing at the end and my conclusion is weak. Next time, when a lab has analysis I don't fully understand, I should start with the analysis on the first day, not the writing.

Friday I didn't do much. I went to the gym, which I'm counting as a win because I've skipped it for two weeks. I also called my mom, which was good. I think I needed a day that wasn't about getting things done, and I'm trying not to feel guilty about it. The planner shows that day as almost empty, and that's okay.

Saturday I tried to write the essay draft and got stuck on the thesis again. I rewrote the first paragraph four times. Each version was slightly different and none of them felt right. I eventually gave up and wrote the body paragraphs first, which worked much better. Once I had the arguments down, the thesis basically wrote itself because I could see what the paragraphs actually had in common. I want to remember this: when the thesis is stuck, skip it and come back. Perfecting the first sentence before anything else exists is how I lose whole afternoons.

Some patterns I'm noticing:

First, my estimates are consistently too low for anything involving analysis or writing, and about right for reading and problem sets. The app says my tasks take about 1.2 times my estimates on average, but that average hides the real pattern. Problem sets are usually on time. Writing and analysis are where I'm off by fifty percent or more. I should estimate those two categories separately and add a real buffer.

Second, my phone is the biggest source of lost time, and it's not even close. Every time I wrote "distraction" in this journal, it was about my phone or messages. The library sessions work because the phone is out of sight. At home I could try leaving it in another room for the first block, since starting is the hardest part and once I'm into something I don't reach for it as much.

Third, I do my best work in the morning and my worst work after my work shifts. My schedule doesn't reflect that at all. I keep planning heavy tasks for the evening because that's when my calendar is empty, but empty doesn't mean useful. I should plan light tasks for the evenings: flashcards, organizing notes, replying to emails. The hard stuff should go before noon whenever I can manage it.

Fourth, the "setting up" problem. Forty minutes on Monday, twenty on Thursday, probably more that I didn't notice. I think it's avoidance dressed up as productivity. A rule could help: the first five minutes of any block have to produce something visible, even a bad sentence or one solved problem.

For next week, my goals are to start every session with my phone in another room, to move reading and writing to mornings, to estimate writing tasks at one and a half times my gut feeling, and to start lab reports with the analysis. I also want to keep this journal going, because writing all of this down made the week make sense in a way the numbers alone didn't. The numbers told me I was over on my estimates. This told me why.

One more thing: I want to be kinder to myself about Friday. Rest is part of the plan, not a failure of it.
